elements.text:
Just curious, during full_node.chain().get_transaction() and .get_block() , is it ever the case that the async callback would be invoked *in the OS thread that this call is made*, i.e. **BEFORE** get_transaction/block() returns -

Or instead, is the callback always run in one of LB’s worker threads?

I was thinking that the optimal speed case would be dispatching the async callback within the self same OS thread as the get_transaction/block() call is made - e.g. in the situations where that transaction or block is already cached - here no work by LibBitcoin worker threads would be needed. This would be the highest possible logical speed possible.

When work is passed from the calling thread to another OS thread, there is a tiny tiny bit of latency for the worker thread to wake up and the memory to move from core to core. Mostly unnoticeable though I guess if you make a billion tx/block requests in a *sequence*, that latency would add up.   Anyhow this was mostly performance trivia.

By the way separately, where in the code do I find how many worker threads full_node* actuall runs?

My thought is, an SSD tends to have is it 32+ queue depth. When the memory mapping accesses the disk, the OS thread blocks. For this reason a full_node for maximum performace, I presume, should have at least 32 OS threads?

elements.text: This qualifies as premature optimization. Until you identify a problem, there is no problem to solve. Increasing the amount of work on a single thread reduces the availability of threads for other work. Load balancing is a performance consideration. Individual calls would certainly be more performant if executed synchronously, as you are essentially suggesting. However this simply blocks other calls, with a subsequent impact on latency of all calls.

A trade off is made with consideration of the thread switching cost against the size of the work. Larger jobs are broken up into smaller jobs, and small jobs are aggregated into larger jobs. The optimal size of any job can only be determined by performance testing. Until you have measured this difference an informed decision on which trade off to make is not possible. Therefore, premature optimization.

elements.text: Libbitcoin is both highly asynchrous and parallel. Many individual std library calls are parallelizable by the compiler, and expensive validation steps (such as script execution) are explicitly parallelized by the implementation. This is also why std lib calls are used when possible vs. for loops. Imposing order where it is not a logical requirement is an antipattern. The same holds for reducing asynchrony to increase individual call performance. This reduces the effectiveness of parallelization.

The guarantee is that it is asynchronous and that callbacks are invoked in the order that events happen. You have to write asynchronous code to use it. You could of course run it on one thread, and it will still be asynchronous, but given only one thread it would not be parallel. You could also just block every callback thread and starve the network pool (to the same effect).

But these are poor choices. If you require order you impose it using critical sections of your own.

elements.text: For example, your handler can block on a mutex until it's complete. That will cause it to process callbacks in order. Just be careful, this type of programming requires a pretty good understanding of parallelism. Code under mutex must have a no-reentrance guarantee or you will most likely deadlock yourself. It's very hard to provide that guarantee except for noting visually that there is a direct path through the critical section.

After running for a long time, the reception of blocks suddenly stops.

According to the log this is the last block it received:

On Linux curiously the exact same program works. So weird.


As you see, threads 15 and 16 are doing an operation at 0xda33452f878 , some kind of contention i guess.
And, threads 17 and 14 are doing a mutex op on 0xda2a38a0a50.


I presume this is a locking related bug, that for some magic reason only appears in this particular environment, i have no idea why =)))
